title: With Due Respect (Vol. 3) -- Ch. 7: CJ Puno and Ombudsman Gutierrez
keywords: the anchor of the Supreme Court
primary_topics: Chapter 7 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 3) -- CJP's January 25, 2009 Inquirer column answering two live questions: whether Chief Justice Reynato Puno should run for president, and whether a private 'citizens' committee' should investigate bribery allegations against DOJ prosecutors

His 'jurist, not politician' answer (prompted by a 17-year-old reader's email): Puno should stay and lead the judiciary in 'defending the Constitution and our democracy,' since both impeachment threats and presidential 'enticements' would 'cut short his term' and 'stain the magistracy' -- 'one may be a good referee' without being 'a boxing champion'

His 'Ombudsman, not citizens' committee' answer: having declined Executive Secretary Ermita's invitation to join such a body, he argues the Office of the Ombudsman was 'precisely conceived by the Constitution' for this, with the fiscal autonomy, independence and coercive powers a citizens' committee lacks

The warning that a citizens' committee would duplicate a constitutional agency, invite court challenges and delays, reflect badly on the self-styled anti-drug 'czarina' President, and 'affront' Ombudsman Merceditas Gutierrez -- who should instead be left to 'show her mettle'
sub_topics: The teenager's question: 17-year-old reader Jerald Jayme emailed to ask whether CJ Puno 'has what it takes to be Philippine president,' prompting CJP's reply praising his civic-mindedness and explaining why Puno should not run

Jurist, not politician: CJP is 'glad' Puno 'definitely said he would not run,' since he has 'so much to do' leading 'the judiciary, not just the Supreme Court, in defending the Constitution and our democracy'; any presidential interest would drag him and 'the institution he represents... to the gutter,' so the judiciary must be 'insulate[d]... from politics'
The referee analogy: 'It takes a different talent to be a politician... One may be a good referee. That does not necessarily mean that the referee can also be a boxing champion'

Why both threats converge: 'the much talked about impeachment of Chief Justice Reynato Puno and the spidery enticements to lure him to the presidential web have a common denominator -- both will cut short his term,' for once he runs he 'would have to resign pronto,' leaving no one to 'save the people from constitutional machinations'

The anchor argument: Puno's call for a 'moral force' is acclaimed, but 'so is the rule of law,' the 'bedrock of our democracy,' 'rooted in the Constitution,' whose guardian is the Supreme Court led by the Chief Justice -- 'absent such leadership, we may not have any election in 2010,' so the country 'cannot afford to lose the anchor of the Supreme Court'

Ombudsman, not citizens' committee: after drug-enforcement officers alleged bribery against some DOJ prosecutors, Executive Secretary Eduardo Ermita twice phoned to invite CJP onto an 'independent... citizens' committee' to investigate, which he 'respectfully declined'

Why the Ombudsman should act: the Office of the Ombudsman was 'precisely conceived by the Constitution' to 'investigate on its own, or on complaint... any act or omission of any public official... illegal, unjust, improper or inefficient,' and Ombudsman Merceditas Gutierrez holds 'plenary power to stop, prevent and correct any abuse' and to 'prosecute, suspend, dismiss or otherwise penalize' -- with fiscal autonomy and independence 'like the judiciary'

Why the committee is wrong: it lacks fiscal autonomy (leaning 'on the generosity of the president') and coercive/contempt powers, duplicates a constitutional agency (so its orders 'may be challenged in court,' causing 'needless complications and delays'), would reflect badly on a President who named herself anti-drug 'czarina' and whose people 'expect instant results,' and is 'an affront to the Ombudsman' -- so 'let the Ombudsman perform her constitutional duty' and 'show her mettle'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 7 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 3), CJP's January 25, 2009 Inquirer column, answers two live questions. First, prompted by a 17-year-old reader's email asking whether Chief Justice Reynato Puno 'has what it takes to be Philippine president,' he gives a 'jurist, not politician' verdict: he is 'glad' Puno 'said he would not run,' because Puno has 'so much to do' leading 'the judiciary... in defending the Constitution and our democracy,' and any presidential interest would drag him and the Court 'to the gutter' -- the judiciary must be 'insulate[d]... from politics.' Talent does not transfer: 'one may be a good referee' without being 'a boxing champion.' Both the impeachment talk and the 'spidery enticements to lure him to the presidential web' share a 'common denominator -- both will cut short his term,' since running would force him to 'resign pronto,' leaving no one to 'save the people from constitutional machinations'; with the rule of law 'the bedrock of our democracy' guarded by the Court under the Chief Justice, the country 'cannot afford to lose the anchor of the Supreme Court' -- 'Puno for president? No.' Second, after drug-enforcement officers alleged bribery against some DOJ prosecutors, Executive Secretary Ermita twice phoned to invite him onto an 'independent... citizens' committee' to investigate, which he 'respectfully declined': the Office of the Ombudsman was 'precisely conceived by the Constitution' to 'investigate on its own... any act or omission of any public official,' and Ombudsman Merceditas Gutierrez holds the 'plenary power to stop, prevent and correct any abuse' with fiscal autonomy and independence 'like the judiciary.' A citizens' committee, by contrast, lacks autonomy and coercive powers, 'duplicates the functions of a constitutional agency' (so its orders 'may be challenged in court,' causing 'needless complications and delays'), would embarrass the self-styled anti-drug 'czarina' President, and is 'an affront to the Ombudsman.' His conclusion: 'No, thank you. Let the Ombudsman perform her constitutional duty. Let her show her mettle and credibility.'
